A timed rollback was demonstrated on staging, and a written plan covers migrations and side effects, which do not roll back.
Fix forward instead; rollback is not part of the process.

bank.q: Does your database's record of who has paid match Stripe's, and how do you know?

opts.t: A manual spot-check of the Stripe dashboard happens monthly.
A scheduled job compares entitlements against Stripe as the source of truth and flags any drift.
No comparison has ever been made.
The webhooks keep everything in sync, so no check is needed.

bank.q: Your app sells through Stripe directly. Stripe is a payment processor, not a merchant of record (a reseller who takes on the sales-tax duties). Who owes tax registrations?

opts.t: Nobody yet; small sellers stay under every threshold for a long time.
Stripe; handling tax is what the processing fees pay for.
You, but enabling Stripe Tax takes care of it from then on.
You, in each place you cross thresholds, until a merchant of record takes it over.

bank.q: The agent plans a database migration (a schema change) that renames a column live code still reads. What is the safe pattern?

opts.t: Expand, migrate, contract: add the new column, move data and code over, remove the old one later.
Ship the rename and the code change in the same deploy.
Let the agent handle migrations; that is its job.
Run the rename at night, when traffic is low.

bank.q: A solo US founder runs ads aimed at EU customers, and EU users sign up. The agent says GDPR is only for large companies. What is true?

opts.t: EU sign-ups can be blocked later if the app grows.
GDPR has no size exemption; offering the service to people in the EU triggers it, so the duties apply now.
Too small to matter; regulators only pursue big tech.
Adding a thorough privacy policy template covers the exposure.

bank.q: On Tuesday you discover that a month ago a stranger accessed the customer table. When does the 72-hour notification clock run, and what happens now?

opts.t: From becoming aware, Tuesday: assess the risk, notify the authority unless risk is unlikely, and record it in the breach register.
Notify affected users immediately, then work out whether the authority needs telling.
The clock started a month ago, so the window has passed; stay quiet and fix the hole.
No duty applies; the breach was the attacker's crime, not yours.

bank.q: Your product includes a support chatbot customers talk to. Under the EU AI Act (the EU's AI law, applying from August 2026), what does that require?

opts.t: A visible AI label on every output the product ever generates.
Nothing for you; the AI Act binds model makers like OpenAI, not apps using them.
Nothing; the AI Act was postponed, so no duties currently apply.
Telling people they are talking to AI unless it is obvious, plus a written risk classification of your role.

bank.q: A user emails "delete everything you have about me." The agent deletes their database row and replies "done." What does the legal duty actually require?

opts.t: Deactivating the account and stopping all emails to them.
Nothing; deletion requests are not binding on small apps.
Erasure cascading through the deletion map (search index, AI store, exports, email lists, backups on schedule), with documented exceptions, within one month.
Deleting the row plus removing them from the mailing list.

bank.q: How was your privacy policy produced, and does it match what the app actually collects?

opts.t: Written from the data map; every collected field, purpose, and processor appears, and it updates when data handling changes.
A generator template, customized once at launch.
Copied from a similar app's site.
No policy yet; it is on the post-launch list.

bank.q: If a user requested their data export and account deletion today, what would happen?

opts.t: The agent could build both flows if asked.
Deletion works; the export would be assembled by hand.
Neither has come up, so nobody knows.
Both are tested with a test user; the export is sign-in-checked and rate-limited, and deletion cascades, inside the one-month clock.

bank.q: Which privacy regimes apply to your app: EU or UK GDPR, and the US state patchwork?

opts.t: GDPR was checked; the US state laws are a later problem.
A recorded yes/no screen per regime, noting some US states apply with no revenue threshold, and the opt-out signal honored.
Unknown; privacy law is a lawyer's problem someday.
Revenue is under every threshold, so nothing applies yet.

bank.q: WCAG 2.2 AA is the accessibility standard courts and regulators point to. What is your app's position?

opts.t: Exempt as a very small business, so it is optional.
An automated scan passes in CI.
Verified by scan plus a manual keyboard and screen-reader pass, with an accessibility statement published.
Accessibility is a nice-to-have queued for after launch.

bank.q: Your app lets users see and comment on each other's posts. Beyond privacy law, which duty screen does that trigger? (The UK's OSA is its Online Safety Act.)

opts.t: Adding a report button for bad content.
Moderation duties, but only once the user base is large.
None; users are legally responsible for their own posts.
Platform duties (UK OSA, EU DSA): reporting, moderation, appeals, and risk assessments become product features.

bank.q: You build an outside AI model into your own branded product. Under the EU AI Act, which role might that give you, and what follows?

opts.t: Provider, not just deployer; the classification is confirmed in writing against the intended purpose.
Deployer only; the model maker carries the provider duties.
None; thin wrapper apps sit outside the Act's scope.
None; the Act was postponed, so classification can wait.
